records.text: On 2023-05-20, the user asked how to monitor a JMX port in Docker Infrastructure with a Zabbix Proxy, how to configure the proxy to communicate with Zabbix Java Gateway, and for an example JMX template.

The assistant suggested deploying a Zabbix Proxy container that can communicate with the Zabbix server, installing Zabbix Java Gateway, configuring the proxy to use the gateway, configuring the Zabbix server to monitor the JMX host through the proxy, linking a JMX template to the host, and verifying connectivity and collected data. It also recommended testing connectivity from the gateway to the target JMX port.

The assistant proposed setting JavaGateway=<gateway IP or hostname> and StartJavaPollers=<number> in zabbix_proxy.conf, then restarting the proxy. It also suggested testing proxy-to-gateway connectivity with telnet or nc and ensuring the proxy and gateway containers share a network or have routing between them. The assistant additionally suggested JavaGatewayPort=<JMX port number>; this was presented as the JMX port, though JavaGatewayPort normally specifies the Java Gateway listening port.

The assistant gave a sample template called “JMX template.” It suggested an item named “JMX Uptime,” with key jmx[java.lang:type=Runtime,name=Uptime], a 60-second update interval, 90-day history, and 365-day trends. It listed additional possible items: heap memory, non-heap memory, thread count, and CPU usage. The response specified item type “Zabbix agent,” although JMX monitoring items ordinarily use the JMX agent item type.

The assistant's sample trigger was named “High CPU Usage,” with expression {JMX template:jmx[java.lang:type=OperatingSystem,name=ProcessCpuLoad].last()}>0.8 and High severity. It also proposed possible triggers for high heap memory, non-heap memory, and thread count, and advised linking the template to the monitored host.

Suggested checks included drum-microphone placement, channel and group EQ/compression and levels, room acoustics, and monitor placement.

For drum-channel EQ on the church’s Midas M32R, suggested starting points were: kick boost around 60–80 Hz and remove rumble below 30 Hz; snare boost around 200–400 Hz for crack and 5–8 kHz for brightness; tom boost around 100–200 Hz for body and 5–7 kHz for attack; overhead and room mics may get a subtle boost around 8–12 kHz for cymbal brightness. These were presented as general starting points to adjust by listening.

Suggested starting compressor settings for the church’s drum channels were: kick attack 10–30 ms, release 100–200 ms, ratio 4:1–6:1; snare attack 5–10 ms, release 100–200 ms, ratio 3:1–5:1; toms attack 10–20 ms, release 100–200 ms, ratio 3:1–5:1; overhead and room microphones attack 10–30 ms, release 100–200 ms, ratio 2:1–3:1. In the 2023-05-24 discussion, VANET was expanded as Vehicular Ad-hoc Network and described as a mobile ad-hoc network in which vehicles communicate with one another and fixed infrastructure over wireless links. The discussion said VANETs aim to improve road safety and traffic efficiency through real-time information and advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS), and can support traffic management, entertainment, and infotainment.
